notes: Uses survival::survreg with a fixed intercept-only formula and four closed distributions. It fits a population baseline, not an individual digital twin.

Declare and select the source treatment group before using a fit as a control baseline. Never infer exposure across an unobserved trial period. Select exactly one time/event row per observed patient; CNSR is a censor indicator and must use statusEncoding=censor. Reconstructed pseudo-IPD retains its source and omitted reconstruction uncertainty.

Median P10/P50/P90 describe delta-method parameter uncertainty, not patient-time percentiles or trial success probabilities. Baseline scenarios hold fitted shape fixed. Only exponential and Weibull currently have patient/design adapters; other fitted curves remain available. Observed survival-time units must agree with the frozen field map.

examples.label: Fit a Weibull baseline to a selected right-censored endpoint

notes: Apply only an immutable source-bound typed equation. Missing predictors, category mappings or units stay unknown; never fill them with zero. Observed predictor units come from the selected frozen field map, while synthetic units are explicit scenario declarations. Source horizon units stay bound to the literal publication.

Equation coefficients are linear-predictor beta. Source bindings explicitly declare coefficientScale=linear_predictor or ratio; positive Cox HR/logistic OR are converted once by log_of_ratio. Apply transform first, then subtract center and divide by scale, both on the transformed predictor scale. For a nonidentity transform, center bindings explicitly declare centerScale=transformed or source_raw; source_raw is converted with the same transform. A Cox equation without baseline survival yields relative scores only. Every centered baseline reference, including zero, needs its preserved numeric binding; standardized zero references remain valid. Baseline centering, horizon and units must match the publication.
Predicted control outcomes are descriptive benchmarks. They do not identify treatment effects, replace observed controls or increase effective sample size.

calibration (optional) holds the applied equation against the outcome the table itself has: outcomeColumn for a linear or logistic equation (a binary outcome is 0/1), timeColumn and statusColumn (1 = event) for a Cox equation. The result then reports the calibration intercept (ideal 0) and slope (ideal 1) with intervals, the observed and the predicted risk and why anything is missing: the slope needs at least 10 events and 10 non-events (10 pairs for a continuous outcome), with fewer only the intercept is reported, and with none of one kind there is no intercept either. The outcome must be observed, never a synthetic or predicted column. It is calibration in this table, not clinical validation, and it says nothing about any other population: the conclusion stays limited.

notes: m is the number of synthetic copies, 5 to 50: fewer than 5 cannot support inference on synthetic data and the engine refuses them. Every copy costs the same again.

Size limit. The copies and their quality scores are made in one R process whose CPU budget is the job's cpuSecondsLimit (the platform's default is 600 s, of which 90% can be used); a job that reaches it fails with no table and no copy kept. The cost grows with the square of the columns for the copies, with the fourth power for the quality score (a logistic model of every pair of columns) and with the square of the rows for its nearest-neighbour check, so a wide table is the expensive one, not a long one. The queue estimates the CPU seconds from the table it will read (rows × columns × m, the subject key not counted) and refuses before queueing a synthesis whose estimate, even divided by the model's worst over-prediction (1.18×), exceeds the budget. A synthesis estimated, with a 1.35× margin, to exceed the budget but not that is queued, and the start says it may not finish and what to reduce.

At the default budget and 5 copies the model allows about 41 columns at 1,000 rows, 35 at 4,000 and 13 at 12,000. The estimate is for numeric, count and 0/1 columns; a text column with many levels costs more.

A refusal, or the notice of a synthesis that may not finish, names what to change: fewer columns (keep only the variables the analysis needs when the field map is built, then freeze a new snapshot), fewer rows (a smaller snapshot), fewer copies down to the minimum, or the job's cpuSecondsLimit where the platform allows more. The engine does not sample rows and does not drop columns, and neither does the queue.

notes: subjectId is the existing population the check is about. `generated` is the population's own profile, filled in by the platform: do not write it (a scenario that carries one is refused). baselineTable is a SECOND baseline table, one that did not make the population, and baselineBindings bind each of its numbers to a verified evidence item exactly as a literature population's do; a table from the same evidence the population was built on is a comparison with the inputs, and the result says so.

Each variable of the table is held against the same variable of the population, by its own distribution: a standardized difference for a continuous or binary variable, the total variation distance for a categorical one, "close" at or under 0.1 and "apart" above it. The joint structure, the shape and the tails of the distributions and any subgroup are not compared, so the result is not a validation of the population; say what it covered and what it did not. referenceN (the second table's sample size, when its source gives it) adds the standard error of each difference.

notes: Arms. Anchored: treatmentColumn is the arm column of the IPD trial (1 = the active arm, 0 = the common comparator) and outcomeColumn the outcome the arms' weighted means are taken of. Unanchored: the IPD patients are the active arm; naming treatmentColumn selects the rows of arm 1 (a table that holds both arms of a trial), without it every row is the active arm. A treatmentColumn the table cannot honour (not in the table, not a complete 1/0 column, no row in arm 1) is reported in diagnostics.notApplied with the reason and every row is used.

Scales. Unanchored: aggregateOutcome and aggregateSe are the aggregate trial's outcome and its standard error on the outcome's OWN scale (a proportion for link logit, a positive mean or rate for link log, any number for identity), the scale of the outcomeColumn's mean; the engine applies the link to the level and the delta method to the standard error. A level outside the link's domain (a proportion not strictly between 0 and 1 on logit, a mean not above 0 on log) is refused (scenario_value_invalid). Anchored: aggregateEstimate and aggregateSe are already the aggregate trial's contrast and its standard error on the link scale (a log odds ratio, a log risk ratio, a mean difference).

anchored false (the default) has no common comparator, so the comparison is unbiased only if every prognostic factor and every effect modifier is among the matched covariates; the result states that as its premise (无锚定：假定所有预后因子和效应修饰因子都已调整). Name the effect modifiers you could not match on in unadjustedEffectModifiers instead of leaving it empty, and report the number as an unanchored comparison, never as an adjusted treatment effect.

notes: tauPrior is the prior on the between-study spread tau, on the analysis scale (a logit for events / n): half_normal has density proportional to exp(-tau^2 / (2 scale^2)), half_cauchy proportional to 1 / (1 + (tau / scale)^2) over the whole half line, and uniform is flat on [0, scale] and zero beyond scale. With two historical studies a half-Cauchy prior leaves the predictive spread without a finite value (diagnostics.tauPrior says so); three or more, or a half-normal prior, make it finite. current.estimate and current.se are on the analysis scale as well: the logit of the control rate (and its standard error on that scale) on the events / n path, the scale of historical.estimate on the estimate / se path.

analysis.method for a two-arm design follows the endpoint: continuous ttest|ancova; binary risk_difference|logistic; time_to_event logrank|rmst|maxcombo.

A single-arm design runs the analysis of its endpoint: single_arm binary exact_binomial, continuous one_sample_t|one_sample_z, time_to_event one_sample_logrank; single_arm_external binary stratified_risk_difference; simon_two_stage binary simon_boundary.

A single-arm trial of a mean or a survival time is compared with a fixed benchmark: truth.benchmark is the historical mean (continuous), truth.controlMedian or truth.controlDistribution the benchmark survival, and truth.effect (the true mean minus the benchmark) or truth.hazardRatio (the trial's hazard over the benchmark's) is the effect, 0 or 1 for the null. analysis.alternative describes that parameter: for a time-to-event endpoint less is a benefit (a hazard below the benchmark's) and greater is harm.

costs: the cost measure is perPatient x N + perSite x sites + perMonth x duration. A duration exists only for a time-to-event design with an accrual block, so a continuous or binary design gets its cost from perPatient and perSite, and a perMonth cost there is declined with its reason (diagnostics.performanceNotComputed).

A frozen Simon two-stage design (simon_two_stage) is simulated at truth.responseRate with its given boundaries n1, r1, n, r. truth.alternativeRate and analysis.alpha do not change that; they are what the result reports the frozen design against: diagnostics.frozenDesign holds its exact rejection probability, early-stop probability and expected sample size at truth.nullRate and at truth.alternativeRate, and, when analysis.alpha is written, whether its type I error is within it.

A hazard ratio that changes over time is simulation-only: truth.treatmentHazardRatios = { breaks, ratios } gives the treatment arm's hazard as ratios[j] times the control's on the j-th interval of breaks (ratios has one more value than breaks, the last runs on), so a delayed effect is breaks [6], ratios [1, 0.6] and a crossing of the curves [6], [1.4, 0.6]. State it INSTEAD of truth.hazardRatio, not beside it; the analytic design (design_analytic) and the assurance refuse it by name. There is then no single true hazard ratio, so bias, mean squared error and coverage are not computed for the log-rank family, and no closed form is drawn for the power; an RMST analysis keeps its bias, against the RMST difference integrated from the two survival curves.

analysis.method maxcombo (time-to-event, two-arm, fixed design only) is the most favourable of the four Fleming-Harrington weighted log-rank statistics G(0,0), G(0,1), G(1,0), G(1,1), its p-value read from their joint null distribution. It is never a default: the analysis is the log-rank unless you say otherwise, because the log-rank is often as good (it loses to MaxCombo mainly when the curves separate late or cross), and the choice is made before the data. Use it only for a hypothesis the person has stated (an effect that starts late, curves that separate late or cross), and run the log-rank beside it. A group-sequential design looks with the log-rank and refuses maxcombo.

From design.grid 1.3.0 the truth scenarios of one design share that design's random stream (common random numbers), where the generator makes that an honest pairing (two-arm designs); designs are never paired with each other and single-arm designs keep independent seeds. A difference between two truths of a design is then a cleaner comparison; each cell is still one immutable run, equal to the design.simulate job at its own seed. A truth that states treatmentHazardRatios replaces the base truth's hazardRatio (and the other way round).

design.allocation is the share allocated to treatment. On a time-to-event endpoint it enters the power calculation. On a continuous or binary endpoint the arms are sized by nTreat and nControl: a stated allocation sizes the control arm when nControl is absent (nControl = nTreat x (1 - allocation) / allocation), and a stated nControl is used as it is, with an allocation it contradicts named in diagnostics.notApplied.

notes: eventTarget counts events among every patient the forecast follows: the patients still to enrol and the patients already enrolled (the sum of explicitly supplied sites[].enrolled design assumptions; no operational ledger is read), so it is at most the target, or the patients already enrolled if there are more (scenario_value_invalid at eventTarget above that). The events of the enrolled patients are simulated, not read: the engine is given no observed event count, so it draws how long each enrolled patient has been followed from how long the site has been open (sites[].exposureTime) and an event time after enrolment from eventHazard; diagnostics.eventForecast says how many events that drew as already happened. With every patient already enrolled, last_patient_in_months is 0 and target_events_months is still forecast. Write eventHazard with eventTarget.
